concepts.hook: A blind ram washed off a trade boat in a squall still swims toward the Unflown, with a length of wool-rope caught round one horn.
Each spring a nanny goat lost from a wrecked boat climbs out of the sea onto the nearest cliff, though no one has ever found her hut.
An otter carries a sail-needle in its teeth and mends the nets of fishers who drowned before finishing them, a gift Ennu is said to have given it.

concepts.gloss: The Hare of the Dead Calm
concepts.hook: A hare runs across flat water where no wind blows, and sailors who see it know they will drift for days, and Tavo never lets it be caught.
An old cod swims with a trader's iron hook through its jaw, and wherever it turns the lines go slack and boats drift onto the Leeward rocks.
A storm-bird rides the wake of the dead down the Leeward road, sleeping on the wind and never once touching the sea.
The drowned spread their wings to dry on the Leeward skerries before flying north, like shags at low tide, and the living are told not to look.
A puffin carries a coin of salt-weight in its beak between the islands and the far trading ports, and it returns only when the price is fair.
A skua snatches fish from gulls in mid-air, and it was set in Vel as a warning to traders who weigh their salt false.
A school of small fish gathers beneath a sinking boat and lights its hull so the crew can find the way down, and it burns on in Vel for their sake.
An octopus creeps into fishing nets at night and unpicks the knots one by one, and the fishers say it is searching the cords for their dead men's names.
A jellyfish drifts on still water far out where no boat should go, and its bell rings faintly when a voyager is about to be lost.
A crab walks the sea floor counting the bones of the drowned, and Hesk, who keeps count, has not yet agreed with its total.
A ray sleeps beneath the hulls in the cold months, warming the keel so the boat does not freeze, and it is paid for with the first catch.

concepts.gloss: The Gull Who Lost a Word
concepts.hook: A messenger gull carrying a prayer to Vel forgot one word on the way and now flies between the Leeward and the islands trying to remember it.
A mouth as wide as a rock pool opens under the reef and takes anchors and oars, and mothers keep their children's names short so it will not hear them.
A thing built of drift, tangled rope and broken weir-stakes walks the tideline on legs of driftwood, and any boat it touches comes home full of sand.
A grey hound with bell-teeth runs the ebb and hunts boats that come in late, and it is said to be a hound Aun once left behind.
A floe closes around boats that drift too far into the cold like a pair of jaws, and the grinding of its ice is a song the drowned hum.
A stalk of kelp rises from the deepest water to the surface, and the drowned climb it at night to look for the lamps of home.
A root torn from some warm far shore drifted in and was planted in the sand, and the wood-carvers who work it say they are carving their own homes.
Sea-moss streams from a dead woman's hair beneath the Leeward waves, and sailors who cut it for their nets bring bad luck to the boat.
The wives of drowned men tie sea-thrift into bundles and drop them from the cliff, and the bundles are said to float north until they reach Hesk's reel.
A flock of fog-sheep grazes low over the Leeward water, and their wool blocks the harbour mouths until Tavo's wind comes to shear it.
Three gusts are tied in a knot and thrown at a boat before dawn, and any sailor who counts them wrong is taken.
A frost-woman knits cloth from sea-spray on the far side of the ice, and she wants a sailor to lend her a needle.
A waterspout rises out of the calm and draws water from a boat the way a woman draws from a well, and it is named for Tavo's thirst.
She beats the sailcloth of trade boats with hail until it stiffens, and the sailors leave her their first bolt of cloth as a gift.
A long eel of lightning coils through the thunderheads over the Leeward shelves and strikes the masts of boats that carry iron.
A thistle grows on the outermost skerry with its roots in salt, and it is said to be the last plant that holds a lost boat to the shore.
